Evolving Agent Interfaces

Saaket Agashe    Yuzhe Yang    Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega    Bhuvan Koduru§    Chih-Lun Li    Jiachen Yang    Ang Li    Xin Eric Wang Corresponding author: =
Abstract

Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents’ trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s

1 Introduction

We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered.

— Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson

Computer-use agents (CUAs) carry out tasks by observing and acting on digital environments. Their interfaces determine what they can observe and which operations they can request. Current computer-use frameworks focus on GUI interaction, supplemented by dedicated tools (Xie et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024). These interfaces are designed by humans and fixed before task execution. Even though these interfaces are built specifically for agents, they still depend on human judgments about what those agents need.

This practice creates three problems for computer-use. First, it ties progress to manual labor. Computer use is open-ended, and each new family of tasks or model release exposes new failure modes. A human researcher must read trajectories, diagnose failures, and use them to write new primitives, observation formats, or memory mechanisms, and then release the result as a new agent framework with a new preset interface. This loop does not scale with task diversity. Second, a static interface often mismatches the task, and current methods compensate with test-time compute instead of a better interface. For example, an agent may complete a shell task by clicking to open a terminal window, typing commands one character at a time, and reading screenshots of a partly occluded terminal for feedback, when a direct shell interface would be faster and more reliable (Yuan et al., 2026; Jia et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025). Additional sampling can raise benchmark scores under such mismatches, but through wasteful and brittle strategies. Third, methods that compose test-time experience into reusable skills or routines inherit the same limit (Agashe et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b). Each skill is a composition of the preset observations and actions. Distillation can reorder what the interface allows, but it cannot extend it. These problems arise because the interface is treated as a design decision that humans make before deployment, and not as an object that can be studied and improved from the agent’s own experience.

Instead, computer-use interfaces should evolve from the agent’s own experience. Therefore, we introduce Agent S411 1 The name reads as Agent Scientist for (4) Evolving Agent Interfaces an autonomous CUA scientist that studies computer-use agents and builds Evolving Agent Interfaces through population-based evolution. Its output is a repository of mixed interfaces and knowledge about when and how to use them. The task agent’s model and harness remain fixed, with the harness governing model invocation, execution, permissions, and task budgets.

The task agent uses candidate repositories of Evolving Agent Interfaces to attempt synthetic tasks, producing trajectories without ground-truth success labels. A meta-agent studies these trajectories and forms hypotheses about how changes to actions, observations, or usage knowledge could help the task agent. It constructs descendants through mutation of one repository or crossover between two. Descendants can add, revise, or remove interfaces and knowledge, and the population retains alternative designs for further development and recombination.

To limit specialization to the tasks that motivated these changes, Agent S4 separates the evidence used for construction from that used for selection. The meta-agent receives training trajectories, while validation instructions, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain hidden from it. Validation performance guides parent selection. We evaluate the final selected repository on the full benchmark. The meta-agent never observes any benchmark task while constructing interfaces, and the validation tasks influence only which repositories are selected during evolution.

We evaluate Agent S4 on OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026) and ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025). On the full 108-task OSWorld V2 set, Qwen3.8-27B with the evolved repository reaches 21.3%21.3\% binary success, above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%13.0\%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%20.6\%) at about 4.3%4.3\% and 1.5%1.5\% of their respective costs. In a separate evolution run on ScienceBoard, which covers niche scientific applications, the evolved repository reaches a 58.6%58.6\% success rate, compared with 41.4%41.4\% for the human-designed interface of Qwen CUA. These results show that agents can evolve their own computer-use interfaces from purely synthetic, verifier-free task experience and outperform human-designed interfaces. We compare our setup against evolutionary baselines such as linear evolution and measure the effect of giving the meta-agent a scratch virtual machine to test its evolved interfaces. Finally, we qualitatively compare agents that act through evolved interfaces with agents that use fixed, human-designed interfaces.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Evolving Agent Interfaces from synthetic, verifier-free experience. We introduce Agent S4, which evolves a repository of interfaces and usage knowledge from synthetic task experience, without success labels or task verifiers, while the task agent’s model and harness stay fixed. Validation tasks the meta-agent never sees decide which repositories to develop further.

  • •

    Evolving interfaces outperform fixed ones. With a repository of interfaces evolved by Agent S4, Qwen3.8-27B exceeds both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 in binary success on OSWorld V2 at a small fraction of their cost, and improves ScienceBoard success over a fixed-interface agent with the same model.

  • •

    Analysis of evolved interfaces. Repository and trajectory analyses show that evolved interfaces change both what the agent observes and how it acts, across desktop-wide, application-specific, cross-application and task-specific interfaces. We also compare evolution strategies, with and without a scratch environment for the meta-agent.

2 Problem Formulation

We study how the interfaces of a computer-use agent can be evolved from task experience. An agent updating a spreadsheet through screenshots must identify visible cells, enter values, and inspect the display to check the result. A structured interface can expose the relevant rows and formulas, accept a bulk edit, and return the changed values. Both interfaces can achieve the same subgoal (Coutaz et al., 1995), but they require different decisions and provide different feedback. Their cost and reliability can also differ. Task experience can reveal which operations are missing, which observations are difficult to use, and where a different interface would help.

We call reusable interfaces that are constructed and improved from task experience Evolving Agent Interfaces. To make interfaces and knowledge available across tasks, we represent them in a persistent repository RR. It contains executable interfaces and supporting knowledge such as capability descriptions, reusable workflows, configuration, and notes about when and how to use them.

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the target distribution of tasks and AA the agent that uses the repository. Let J⁡(A,R,x)J(A,R,x) denote the expected task score when AA uses repository RR to attempt task xx. We seek a repository constructed from task experience that maximizes this score across tasks,

R⋆∈arg⁡maxR​𝔼x∼𝒟​[J⁡(A,R,x)].R^{\star}\in\arg\max_{R}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[J(A,R,x)\right]. (1)

This objective concerns performance beyond the experience used to construct the repository. We next define the agent, interfaces, and interaction process that determine JJ.

Computer and task.

A computer CC has a state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} comprising its files, running applications, displays, services, and reachable network endpoints. A task x=(g,s0,Vx,Bx)x=(g,s_{0},V_{x},B_{x}) consists of an instruction gg, an initial state s0s_{0}, an evaluator VxV_{x} that scores the outcome, and a budget BxB_{x}.

Interface.

An interface I=⟨cI,𝒜I,𝒪I⟩I=\langle c_{I},\mathcal{A}_{I},\mathcal{O}_{I}\rangle connects an agent to one or more parts cIc_{I} of the computer through a language of requests 𝒜I\mathcal{A}_{I} and a language of observations 𝒪I\mathcal{O}_{I}. Executing a request can change the state and returns an observation, (s′,o)∼TI(⋅∣s,a)(s^{\prime},o)\sim T_{I}(\cdot\mid s,a). A GUI interface, for example, accepts clicks and keystrokes and returns screenshots. A shell interface accepts bash commands and returns a string with the requested information, return values or error message.

Model, harness, and agent.

A model MM is a language model that generates responses and requests conditioned on its input context. A harness HH manages model invocation, request execution, task budgets, permissions PHP_{H}, and preparation of the model’s context, including any context compaction. An agent A=(M,H)A=(M,H) is the model operating through this harness. The agent initially has access to a base set of interfaces ℐ\mathcal{I}. The harness executes requests through these interfaces and places the resulting observations in the model’s context. For example, the harness can execute a spreadsheet helper under a time limit and permission boundary. The helper defines the requests for reading or editing cell ranges and the values returned to the agent. The harness governs execution, while the interface specifies the available operations and feedback.

Computer use.

Computer use is the process through which an agent observes and acts on a computer through available interfaces to accomplish a task. The interaction history hth_{t} records the interfaces, requests, and observations from earlier steps. At step tt, the agent chooses an interface and a request based on the instruction and this history, with context preparation by HH left implicit,

(It,at)∼M(⋅∣g,ht,ℐ),(st+1,ot)∼TIt(⋅∣st,at).(I_{t},a_{t})\sim M(\cdot\mid g,h_{t},\mathcal{I}),\qquad(s_{t+1},o_{t})\sim T_{I_{t}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}). (2)

The available interfaces shape which operations the agent can request and what evidence it receives about their effects.

Formally, R=(ℐ⁡(R),K⁡(R))R=(\mathcal{I}(R),K(R)), where ℐ⁡(R)\mathcal{I}(R) contains its executable interfaces and K⁡(R)K(R) its supporting knowledge. The repository supplies interfaces ℐR=ℐ∪ℐ⁡(R)\mathcal{I}_{R}=\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}(R) and knowledge that informs the agent’s choices,

(It,at)∼M(⋅∣g,ht,ℐR,K(R)).(I_{t},a_{t})\sim M(\cdot\mid g,h_{t},\mathcal{I}_{R},K(R)). (3)

Each attempt is subject to the task budget BxB_{x} and harness permissions PHP_{H}. The score J⁡(A,R,x)J(A,R,x) averages the evaluator’s score over these interactions.

Interface evolution.

Interfaces implemented as programs can be revised like any other software. A program can export a material schedule through Blender’s Python API, extract selected rows from a Calc workbook, or return supplier prices gathered through a sequence of browser operations. Each defines its own requests and observations (Wang et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2023). Because these interfaces are code, an agent that can read trajectories and write code can redesign them. It can decide which operations to combine, what information to return, and how a result can be checked. We call this process interface evolution. Given a repository RkR_{k} and the trajectories 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k} of the agent using it, an evolution step produces a revised repository,

Rk+1=E⁡(Rk,𝒯k).R_{k+1}=E\!\left(R_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k}\right). (4)

Task experience guides each step. Repeated reconstruction of the same calculation across tasks can motivate a reusable operation, and a repeated inability to verify a change can motivate a new observation. Trajectories with the revised repository then provide evidence for further revision. Section 3 instantiates EE with population-based evolution.

3 Agent S4

Agent S4 builds Evolving Agent Interfaces and usage knowledge through population-based evolution of repositories, keeping the task agent’s model MM and harness HH fixed. Each iteration selects parents from a population, constructs a descendant through mutation or crossover, evaluates it, and adds it to the population while retaining its parents (Figure 3). Training experience guides the repository changes, and held-out validation guides subsequent selection. This optimizes Equation 1 for the fixed task agent AA. Algorithm 1 gives the procedure.

3.1 Population and selection

The population contains repository variants, each with its own interfaces and knowledge. We initialize ℛ0={R0}\mathcal{R}_{0}=\{R_{0}\} from a seed repository (Appendix A.2) and evaluate it to obtain training trajectories and a validation score. These records are retained with each candidate as the population grows.

At each step, an operator schedule chooses mutation or crossover. Mutation requires one parent, and crossover requires two distinct parents. For each parent, binary tournament selection draws two eligible variants uniformly and chooses the one with the higher validation score. A sole eligible candidate is selected directly. For crossover, the first selected parent is excluded from the second selection. The selected repositories and their saved training trajectories provide the starting point for the next descendant.

3.2 Mutation and crossover

The meta-agent Ameta=(Mmeta,Hmeta)A_{\mathrm{meta}}=(M_{\mathrm{meta}},H_{\mathrm{meta}}) constructs descendants using a fixed model and harness. Its computer CmetaC_{\mathrm{meta}} holds the selected parent repositories, their training trajectories, and a lineage notebook in its filesystem. It studies the recorded behavior and observations to diagnose apparent failures and inefficiencies and form hypotheses about useful changes. For example, repeated cell-by-cell edits can motivate a bulk spreadsheet interface, while poor use of an existing interface can motivate revised usage knowledge. It implements these hypotheses through file, shell, and code interfaces using one of two operators.

Mutation.

Starting from one parent RpR_{p}, the meta-agent adds, revises, or removes interfaces and knowledge. Changes can affect operations, returned observations, and reusable workflows, including capabilities inherited from the seed.

Crossover.

Given two distinct parents RaR_{a} and RbR_{b}, the meta-agent constructs one coherent descendant by choosing between overlapping interfaces, porting complementary capabilities, or combining their ideas into new code and knowledge. The descendant need not contain the union of its parents.

Both operators produce a single descendant repository R′R^{\prime}. The fixed base access ℐ\mathcal{I} remains unchanged as the repository’s interfaces ℐ⁡(R)\mathcal{I}(R) and knowledge K⁡(R)K(R) evolve.

3.3 Evaluation and population update

After construction, we freeze R′R^{\prime} and run the fixed task agent AA on synthetic training tasks 𝒯train\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{train}} and disjoint validation tasks 𝒯val\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{val}}. The repository is available in the task agent’s filesystem, and a fixed prompt identifies its location and explains how to discover its capabilities. The agent can consult its documentation and source code and invoke the interfaces it selects through the harness’s existing code-execution tool (Appendix A.2). Each rollout τ∼Rollout⁡(A,R′,C,x)\tau\sim\operatorname{Rollout}(A,R^{\prime},C,x) starts from task xx’s initial state within its budget and records the instruction, interfaces, requests, and observations. The repository remains fixed during execution. Temporary programs written by the agent do not persist across tasks.

Training experience and validation score.

Training trajectories have no ground-truth success labels. We save them as evidence for future repository changes and reuse them whenever the descendant becomes a parent. Validation rollouts provide a separate selection score for each candidate RR,

Fval​(R)=1|𝒯val|​∑x∈𝒯valVx​(Rollout⁡(A,R,C,x)).F_{\mathrm{val}}(R)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{val}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{val}}}V_{x}\!\left(\operatorname{Rollout}(A,R,C,x)\right). (5)
Asymmetric evaluation.

Only training trajectories are exposed to the meta-agent. Validation tasks, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain inaccessible to it. Validation therefore influences construction through parent selection, without supplying direct feedback for repository edits.

Adding the descendant.

We add R′R^{\prime} to the population alongside its parents regardless of its validation score. This retains alternative designs for further development and recombination. Parent links form a directed acyclic graph, with one parent per mutation and two per crossover. Optional pruning removes parent eligibility while preserving lineage records. The updated population supplies candidates for the next iteration. After NN steps, we select a member of ℛN\mathcal{R}_{N} by validation performance, using a benchmark-specific criterion (Section 4), and freeze it for evaluation on target tasks 𝒯test\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{test}}. The meta-agent observes none of these tasks during construction, and validation tasks drawn from the same benchmark affect only selection.

4 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and task sets.

OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026) is our primary benchmark, and ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025) tests generalization to niche scientific computer-use applications and workflows. Repository evolution uses 30 synthetic training tasks for OSWorld V2 and 48 for ScienceBoard, plus 15 official validation tasks for each. Synthetic task attempts yield trajectories without ground-truth success labels. The meta-agent receives these training trajectories. Validation scores guide selection, but validation trajectories and evaluators remain outside its evidence. Full-benchmark results cover 108 OSWorld V2 and 169 ScienceBoard tasks, including the 15 validation tasks of each. Benchmark details appear in Appendix A, and synthetic task construction is described below and in Appendix D.

Model and harness.

On both benchmarks, the task agent and meta-agent use Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) in a modified Prime Agent harness (Karten et al., 2026) that executes code in a persistent IPython kernel, with Medium reasoning, a 131,072-token context window, a 32,000-token output limit, and automatic context compaction. The model and harness remain fixed within each search. Appendix A gives the harness version, sampling parameters, and compaction settings; Appendix C gives implementation constraints and builder prompts.

Baselines.

On OSWorld V2, we evaluate the task agent with no repository, the seed repository, and the evolved repository, and compare against Qwen CUA.22 2 We use the Qwen CUA implementation provided by OSWorld V2: https://github.com/xlang-ai/OSWorld-V2/tree/main/mm_agents/qwen. On ScienceBoard, we compare the seed and evolved repositories with Qwen CUA. Qwen3.8-27B results come from our own evaluations. Results for other models in Figure 2 and Table 2, including per-task costs, are taken from Table 3 of Yuan et al. (2026).

Evolution baselines.

Table 1 summarizes the four evolution baselines, all starting from the same seed repository. Each construction step produces one descendant. Seed evaluation and validation re-evaluations are not construction steps. The OSWorld V2 searches share the same training and validation sets.

Population search alternates mutation (one parent) and crossover (two distinct parents), starting with mutation. Binary tournaments choose parents from the eligible population using mean partial validation score on OSWorld V2 and validation success on ScienceBoard. After 10 steps, the five lowest-scoring variants are removed from parent eligibility. Linear evolution mutates the latest descendant at every step, without tournament selection or crossover.

A scratch VM with the same AMI as the benchmark tasks lets the meta-agent inspect running applications and try interface code during construction. Without it, the meta-agent works from repository code and saved training trajectories. In all four settings, task agents execute in benchmark VMs. Each meta-agent construction has a two-hour wall-clock budget for OSWorld v2 and 1 hour wall clock budget for ScienceBoard.

Validation and repository selection.

On OSWorld V2, we select the repository that fully solves the most validation tasks and break ties by mean partial validation score, since binary success is the harder metric to improve. On ScienceBoard, whose evaluator reports only success, we select the repository with the highest validation success rate.

In the case of Scienceboard, we also run a Denoise operation after every 5 steps. This picks the top-3 variants in the population and reevaluates them. The repositories validation score is then replaced by the updated running average. We analyze the effect of this denoising step in Section 7.3. We do not run the denoising step for OSWorld-v2 due to much longer time and cost of evolution and repeated evaluations.

Evaluation budgets and cost.

Prime Agent task rollouts have a 300-step budget on both benchmarks, where a step is one completed assistant response and can contain multiple actions. New OSWorld V2 training and validation rollouts also have a two-hour wall-clock limit. The final evaluation keeps the step budget but has no per-task wall-clock limit. ScienceBoard applies a 60-minute wall-clock limit to training, validation, validation repeats, and full evaluation.

We report binary success and partial score on OSWorld V2 and success rate on ScienceBoard. OSWorld V2 task-solving costs are estimated from model-token usage at Parasail’s input and output rates, assuming an 80%80\% input-cache hit rate, and exclude repository construction and runtime infrastructure. Appendix A lists the rates and remaining runtime settings.

Synthetic task construction.

We constructed 30 synthetic tasks for OSWorld V2 and 50 for ScienceBoard, of which 48 are used (Appendix E), giving Agent S4 task experience for evolving Agent Interfaces and usage knowledge without ground-truth success labels. Tasks follow each benchmark’s methodology but use independently authored scenarios. For OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026), we studied its task-construction principles and challenge-phenomenon taxonomy, and scaled the reported counts of overlapping phenomena into approximate targets for our 30 tasks. These targets guided the representation of capabilities such as cross-source reasoning, visual-spatial precision, and implicit-state inference. For ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025), we followed a planned distribution across six scientific applications and preserved its compact tasks, usually centered on one application and one meaningful outcome.

Tasks were created agentically by a coordinator (GPT-6 Astra), authors (GPT-5.6-Sol), and independent reviewers (GPT-5.6-Sol). The coordinator tracked accepted tasks against the planned counts and assigned new tasks to phenomena or applications below target. Each author started from a fresh context with application documentation, design requirements, and summaries of accepted synthetic tasks, but without access to official task instances, evaluators, or task-agent trajectories. Authors produced instructions, input artifacts, and environment setup specifications, documenting provenance and capability assumptions.

Reviewers checked originality, coherence, feasibility, and appropriate complexity. To ensure that no synthetic task overlaps with an existing benchmark task, they compared each candidate’s purpose, dependencies, operations, and deliverables against official instruction and setup metadata and against the accepted synthetic set. Each claimed challenge had to be supported by the actual materials. The coordinator returned concrete defects for up to two revision rounds, rejected overlapping designs, and kept official comparisons out of author feedback. Automated input and setup checks supplemented these reviews, and only accepted versions entered the training set. No step graded task-agent attempts or produced reference solutions.

5 Main Results

With a repository of interfaces evolved by Agent S4, a 27B open-source model reaches the highest binary success on open-source models at a small fraction of frontier-model cost. Table 2 compares results on the full OSWorld V2 benchmark. We report the best repositories from population evolution with and without a scratch VM, alongside the Qwen CUA baseline and reported open-source and closed-source results from OSWorld V2, which retain the single-action and batched-action settings of the reference evaluations. Binary success measures complete task execution, partial score measures intermediate progress, and cost covers task-solving model calls. Binary gains are the hardest to obtain on OSWorld V2. Strong agents reach similar partial progress, and what separates them is turning that progress into fully completed tasks (Yuan et al., 2026). With the repository evolved without a scratch VM, Qwen3.8-27B achieves 21.30%21.30\% binary success at $1.10 per task, above the 13.00%13.00\% of GPT-5.5 and the 20.60%20.60\% of Claude Opus 4.8 with batched actions, at 4.3%4.3\% and 1.5%1.5\% of their $25.50 and $72.40 costs. With the repository evolved with a scratch VM, it reaches a partial score of 51.06%51.06\% at $1.27 per task.

Evolving interfaces improve the same model. Agents with fixed interfaces already seek programmatic access (Yuan et al., 2026). Terminal commands account for 24.7%24.7\% of their actions, and GPT-5.5 devotes 78%78\% of its budget to code, API, or file operations (Yuan et al., 2026, Section 4). Under a fixed interface, each such program is typed through the desktop and its result is read from a screenshot. Acting through agent evolved interfaces removes this indirection, and the evolved repository supplies interfaces for the applications and data that recur across tasks. Compared with the Qwen CUA baseline, which runs the same Qwen3.8-27B model with fixed interfaces, this raises binary success from 5.56%5.56\% to 21.30%21.30\% and partial score from 20.69%20.69\% to 46.90%46.90\%, or to 51.06%51.06\% with the repository evolved with a scratch VM, while lowering task-solving cost from 1.39​t​o1.39to1.10 per task.

6 Generalization

We next ask whether Agent S4 carries over to a different domain. ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025) contains 169 tasks across six scientific applications. These are Celestia for astronomy, ChimeraX for molecular visualization, GRASS GIS for geographic analysis, KAlgebra for algebra and plotting, Lean for theorem proving and TeXstudio for typesetting. General computer-use interfaces rarely cover these applications, and many of their operations are hard to carry out through clicks alone. We run a fresh evolution with the same task agent, Qwen3.8-27B in Prime Agent, starting from the same seed repository as on OSWorld V2. The meta-agent learns from 48 synthetic training tasks across the six applications (Appendix E), and 15 validation tasks guide selection over 30 construction steps.

Table 3 reports results on the full benchmark. Evolution raises success from 55.03%55.03\% with the seed repository to 58.58%58.58\%, solving 99 of 169 tasks compared with 93, and reduces the average number of model calls per task from 61.7 to 58.9. The selected repository grows from 15 functions in the seed to 64. The additions include a ChimeraX command interface, GRASS GIS modules that run in the live session and a KAlgebra calculator that evaluates many expressions in one call. The gains are largest on KAlgebra, where success rises from 48%48\% to 68%68\%. These results show that Agent S4 can evolve useful interfaces for specialized scientific software from synthetic training experience.

7 Analysis

7.1 Evolution Dynamics

Seed repository and evolution. The first two rows of Table 4 show the task agent with no repository and with the seed repository. The seed raises binary success from 15.74%15.74\% to 19.44%19.44\% while leaving partial score nearly unchanged (44.93%44.93\% versus 44.90%44.90\%), and lowers task-solving cost from $1.36 to $1.11 per task. Evolution without a scratch VM then raises binary success to 21.30%21.30\% and partial score to 46.90%46.90\% at nearly the same cost ($1.10). The seed therefore provides a useful starting point, and evolution improves it on binary success and partial score.

Evolution strategies. We compare three ways of evolving the repository. The first is population-based evolution with a scratch virtual machine (VM), in which the meta-agent can open applications and test interfaces. The second is population-based evolution without the scratch VM. The third is linear evolution with a scratch VM, in which the meta-agent keeps refining each new child repository. With a scratch VM, population-based evolution reaches the same binary success as linear evolution (19.44%19.44\%) and a higher partial score (51.06%51.06\% versus 47.17%47.17\%). Without a scratch VM, population-based evolution reaches the highest binary success (21.30%21.30\%) but a lower partial score (46.90%46.90\%). The scratch VM therefore improves partial progress, while the best binary success comes from evolution without it.

7.2 Qualitative Study of Evolved Interfaces

A taxonomy of evolved interfaces.

To compare runs, we label each interface by the part of the computer it covers and the purpose it serves. The four labels can overlap:

  • •

    System-wide interfaces cover the desktop and operating system as a whole, such as inspecting windows or launching and monitoring background processes.

  • •

    App-specific interfaces expose the objects of one named application, such as spreadsheet ranges in LibreOffice, tracks in a REAPER audio project, or molecules in ChimeraX.

  • •

    Cross-App interfaces work on data or platforms shared by many applications, such as reading and rendering PDF files regardless of which application created them, or reading pages on any website.

  • •

    Task-specific interfaces package a procedure for a particular goal together with a check of whether it is achieved, such as checking a Lean proof, compiling it, updating the editor and reporting completion.

Interfaces also grow after they are introduced, so we label each added operation separately. For example, the office-document interface is App-specific because it edits documents through LibreOffice itself, but an operation added to it later that edits OpenDocument files directly, without the application, is Cross-App. Figure 4 counts new interfaces and these later extensions separately. Table 7 in Appendix B.3 gives examples of evolved interfaces, with what each lets the agent observe and do.

On OSWorld V2 without a scratch VM, evolution introduces four new interfaces and 127 extensions, including 29 System-wide, 63 App-specific and 40 Cross-App extensions. An interface or extension can carry more than one label, so the counts per label can add up to more than the total. Most of its growth therefore deepens interfaces the agent already has. With a scratch VM, where the meta-agent can open applications and test its code, the population introduces 12 new interfaces and 253 extensions. Nine of the new interfaces are App-specific and nine are Cross-App. Seven carry both labels, such as the interfaces for editing musical scores, audio projects and 3D scenes, which operate one application while reading and writing file formats that other applications share. Cross-App extensions rise to 129. These additional application interfaces are a likely explanation for the higher partial score of the best repository evolved with a scratch VM.

On ScienceBoard, evolution introduces seven new interfaces and 91 extensions. Six of the new interfaces and 77 of the extensions are App-specific, for scientific applications such as ChimeraX, KAlgebra, GRASS GIS and Lean. Its three Task-specific extensions package procedures for displaying a map in GRASS GIS and completing a proof in Lean.

Across all three runs, evolved interfaces let the agent observe the desktop, an application’s own objects, data shared across applications, and whether a goal has been met, and act on each of these in a single call. Evolution therefore widens the range of software the agent can operate and raises the level at which it sees, acts and checks its progress.

Case Study: Using the evolved browser interface to handle web data search and fetching instead of a fixed interface.

Figure 5 follows the information-gathering portion of OSWorld V2 task 008, which requires receipts and corresponding card charges for an expense claim. The fixed-interface Qwen CUA agent opens receipt emails one at a time, handles five browser download warnings, and twice tries to open an invoice before its download has finished. Finding the $500 NeurIPS charge also requires eight scrolls and four clicks on Load more. With the evolved repository, the task agent uses browser.api to retrieve mailbox contents and attachment URLs as structured data. It downloads three PDFs with curl, reads them with pdftotext, and reuses the browser interface to query the bank dashboard and cross-check the charges. The agent combines a reusable browser interface with existing command-line tools to gather evidence across applications, reducing repeated visual navigation and manual download handling.

Appendix B.5 provides the more illustrated examples of agents benefitting from using an evolved interface for applications like MailHub, XMind, Zotero, ReviewSphere, and Word tracked changes.

7.3 Repeated Validation during Evolution

Long-horizon computer-use tasks show substantial run-to-run variance (Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026), so a single validation run can overrate a repository. On ScienceBoard, we therefore re-evaluate the three highest-scoring repositories every five steps and score each by the mean of its evaluations (Section 4). Figure 6 shows why this matters. Repositories if-003 and if-004 reach the highest first score, 73.33%73.33\%, at steps 3 and 4. A second evaluation lowers their means to 60.00%60.00\% and 66.67%66.67\%. The selected repository, if-016, scores 73.33%73.33\%, 66.67%66.67\%, 73.33%73.33\% and 73.33%73.33\% across four evaluations, for a mean of 71.67%71.67\%. A first score alone would have ranked if-003 among the best repositories even though its mean is 60.00%60.00\%.

8 Related Work

Computer-use agents and interaction design.

Computer-use systems differ in how they expose observations and actions, and SWE-agent showed that this agent-computer interface shapes performance (Yang et al., 2024). Agent S and Agent S2 organize planning, perception, and action through engineered agent components (Agashe et al., 2025a; Agashe et al., 2025b), while UI-TARS learns policies for GUI interaction (Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a). Other systems add programmatic access beside GUI actions, through application APIs (Lu et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026a), code execution (Song et al., 2025a), or tool calls (Yang et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2026). Agent S3 and its behavior judge improve task completion by selecting among multiple rollouts (Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2025). In these systems, code and tools, when available, are one action among a predefined set. Agents that act only by writing and running code can outperform agents that choose from predefined actions (Wang et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2026). These interfaces are designed by people or written within a single task. Agent S4 instead evolves them across tasks and retains the resulting operations and usage knowledge in a repository that can be developed beyond the task that motivated a change.

Skills, memory, and tool construction.

Reflexion stores textual feedback for later attempts (Shinn et al., 2023), and Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable procedures from experience (Wang et al., 2025b). Reuse can also take executable form. LLMs as Tool Makers separates tool construction from subsequent tool use (Cai et al., 2024), and SkillWeaver discovers and practices web interactions to build APIs that other agents can reuse (Zheng et al., 2025). CUA-Skill instead provides an engineered library of parameterized computer-use skills and composition graphs (Chen et al., 2026). These methods establish that agents can benefit from persistent knowledge and executable tools. Our search operates over complete repository versions containing interfaces, observation routines, configuration, and usage knowledge. Mutation and crossover can change these components together, with selection based on their combined effect on task-agent performance.

Automated agent design and evolutionary search.

ADAS searches for agent designs expressed in code (Hu et al., 2025), and the Darwin Gödel Machine modifies its own coding agent while maintaining an archive of alternatives (Zhang et al., 2025). Self-Harness studies execution traces, proposes harness changes, and validates them through regression tests (Zhang et al., 2026b). AlphaEvolve and ShinkaEvolve combine model-generated code changes with evolutionary search and executable evaluation (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2025), while GEPA uses trajectory reflection to evolve prompts and combine complementary improvements (Agrawal et al., 2025). Validation-based control of overfitting also predates language-model agents, including evolutionary curtailment in genetic programming (Fitzgerald and Ryan, 2011). Agent S4 evolves repositories of interfaces and knowledge through population-based search with asymmetric access to evaluation evidence. The meta-agent studies synthetic-task trajectories without ground-truth success labels and implements changes to application-specific operations, capability descriptions, and reusable workflows. The fixed harness retains control of model invocation, execution, permissions, and budgets. Keeping capabilities in the repository makes them available for revision, selection, recombination, and reuse with compatible agents and harnesses. Validation tasks, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain with the controller and are hidden from the meta-agent. Held-out performance determines which variants become parents, applying selection pressure beyond the tasks used to construct the software.

9 Conclusion

We presented Agent S4, which treats interface design as an agent capability: a meta-agent studies computer-use trajectories to construct and evolve reusable interfaces and knowledge about when and how to use them. The experience used for interface construction comes entirely from synthetic tasks, without ground-truth success labels or task verifiers; separate held-out validation guides repository selection. Qwen3.8-27B with a repository of interfaces evolved by Agent S4 reaches 21.3%21.3\% binary success on the full 108-task OSWorld V2 benchmark, above both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, at about 4.3%4.3\% and 1.5%1.5\% of their reported task-solving costs. On the full 169-task ScienceBoard benchmark, a separate evolution run reaches 58.58%58.58\% success, compared with 41.4%41.4\% for Qwen CUA. Repository and trajectory analyses show how evolution constructs application interfaces and refines the operations and observations available to subsequent task agents. These findings support learning interfaces from synthetic experience as a way to improve computer use while keeping the task agent’s model and harness fixed, complementary to advances in both.

Appendix A Experimental Design

A.1 Benchmark Detail

OSWorld V2. OSWorld V2 (Yuan et al., 2026) evaluates computer-use agents on 108 long-horizon workflows spanning everyday and professional activities in real desktop and web applications. Tasks require agents to combine information across sources, track application state, and adapt to changes during execution. The benchmark reports both binary task completion and partial scores, measuring whether agents can complete an entire workflow and how much of its requirements they satisfy. We use it as our primary benchmark for evaluating repository evolution on complex computer-use tasks.

ScienceBoard. ScienceBoard (Sun et al., 2025) evaluates autonomous agents in realistic scientific workflows involving professional software. It contains 169 human-curated tasks across scientific domains such as biochemistry, astronomy, and geoinformatics. These tasks combine scientific reasoning with software operation through graphical and command-line interfaces, testing whether agents can translate domain-specific instructions into successful execution in scientific environments. We use ScienceBoard to evaluate whether repository evolution extends to specialized scientific applications.

A.2 Settings

Task subsets.

The four evolution runs and their construction budgets are summarized in Table 1. OSWorld V2 uses all 30 authored synthetic tasks. ScienceBoard uses 48 of the 50 authored tasks: we exclude sb_grassgis_010, whose initialization fails a region check, and sb_chimerax_006, whose input file fails to open in ChimeraX. These exclusions concern task initialization, before task-agent execution. Each benchmark uses 15 official tasks for validation. The full reported sets contain 108 OSWorld V2 tasks and 169 ScienceBoard tasks, including those validation tasks.

Comparison interfaces and harnesses.

The interface column in Table 2 describes the execution access exposed to the task agent. All external reference results use the OSWorld V2 reference harness with screenshot observations and a 500-step budget (Yuan et al., 2026, Section 3.1). Claude Opus and Sonnet use the native Claude computer-use interface; GPT-5.5, MiniMax M3, Kimi K2.6, and Qwen3.7-Plus use the benchmark’s PyAutoGUI action backend. The released GPT and MiniMax adapters translate structured computer actions into PyAutoGUI commands; this backend does not imply an unrestricted Python execution tool.33 3 Released GPT and MiniMax adapters in the benchmark’s v2026.06.24 release. These establish available adapter behavior, rather than exact launch configurations for every reported model version. The paper establishes the action backend for Kimi K2.6 and Qwen3.7-Plus, but the public sources do not establish their exact scored-run adapters. We label these reference interfaces Fixed: their requests and observations are set before the task. This describes the interaction surface, not a prohibition on running programs through desktop applications; such programs are entered through the GUI and their output is observed in screenshots.

Our Qwen CUA baseline uses the upstream Qwen harness, with structured computer_use actions for mouse, keyboard, and screenshot control translated into PyAutoGUI. Our Prime Agent conditions instead expose persistent IPython execution, supporting Python and shell code for GUI, file, and API operations. We label these interfaces Extensible: programs the agent writes during a task become additional interfaces whose output returns directly to the agent. The seed and evolved conditions add repository interfaces accessible through this same tool, as described below.

Harness.

For our OSWorld V2 and ScienceBoard repository-evolution experiments, we use a modified harness based on Prime Agent version 0.8.0-beta.546.1.a9b5d88,44 4 https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-agent/releases an IPython-backed coding agent. The harness prompts are reproduced in Appendix C. The model issues tool calls containing Python code, which the harness executes in a persistent IPython kernel and returns the execution outputs to the model for the next step. Variables, imports, and function definitions persist across calls, allowing the agent to reuse intermediate results and invoke repository interfaces throughout a task. Prime Agent’s native threshold-based context compaction is enabled within the 131,072-token context window. The harness reserves 36,096 tokens for the 32,000-token output budget and a 4,096-token overhead margin. Compaction is triggered when the last observed token usage plus the estimated trailing messages exceeds 94,976 tokens. It summarizes older conversation history while retaining the most recent 20,000 tokens verbatim. Prime Agent also automatically rescales oversized images to fit within 2000×20002000\times 2000 pixels while preserving aspect ratio, with further compression or downscaling as needed to keep the base64-encoded payload below 4.5 MiB. We disable Prime Agent’s automatic harness refinement. The task agent can still record notes in the harness state during a task, but this state is deleted before every task, so the repository is the only state that carries over between tasks.

Repository access.

For OSWorld V2, each candidate repository is installed at /home/user/shadow_interface/. A fixed task-agent prompt supplies this path, directs the agent to inspect the toolkit, and encourages its use as the primary approach. The agent invokes python3 -m shadow_interface through the harness’s IPython tool. The capabilities subcommand lists interfaces with signatures and short descriptions; doc <module>.<function> displays full documentation, and call <module>.<function> [args ...] invokes an interface. The prompt also directs the agent to read the source code when the documentation is insufficient. These files expose the repository’s interfaces and usage knowledge without changing the harness’s tool set.

Seed repository.

All three evolution runs in this paper, on OSWorld V2 with and without a scratch VM and on ScienceBoard, start from the same seed repository. It has about 550 lines of Python and shell and offers 15 basic interfaces in four modules (Table 5). They wrap common desktop tools and the Chrome DevTools endpoint, and none is specific to a benchmark application. A setup script installs the tools these interfaces rely on, and a command-line entry point provides the capabilities, doc and call subcommands described above. Every interface, module and usage note in an evolved repository beyond these was added during evolution.

Model Service.

We access Qwen3.8-27B through Parasail provider. We set temperature to 1, top-pp to 0.9, and thinking effort to Medium, with a 131,072-token context window and a 32,000-token output limit. The same model is used for the task agent, GUI grounding, and the interface builder. We estimate task-solving costs using Parasail’s rates of $0.24 per million uncached input tokens, $2.20 per million output tokens, and $0.05 per million cached input tokens. The cost estimates assume an 80% input-cache hit rate. The Qwen3.8-27B cost estimates in Table 2 use these rates. These estimates cover task-solving model calls; repository-evolution and runtime infrastructure costs are excluded.

Cloud infrastructure.

For OSWorld V2, each task episode runs in a freshly initialized virtual machine on AWS using the same benchmark release image, with a screen resolution of 1920×10801920\times 1080 pixels. The virtual machine is terminated after the episode. Model inference is accessed through the API described above.

Runtime settings.

Our Prime Agent task rollouts use a budget of 300 completed assistant responses per task, with a timeout of 720 seconds for each model API call. A response may invoke code that performs multiple GUI or application actions. New OSWorld V2 training and validation rollouts have a two-hour wall-clock limit. OSWorld V2 full evaluation retains the API-call timeout and 300-step budget without a per-task wall-clock limit. ScienceBoard uses a 60-minute wall-clock limit in training, initial validation, validation re-evaluations, and full evaluation. The meta-agent has a separate two-hour wall-clock limit for each repository construction. Infrastructure failures may trigger recovery runs.

Appendix B Experimental Analysis

B.1 Evolution Lineage

Figure 7 shows the repository lineage for the 30-step OSWorld V2 population run with a builder scratch VM. Starting from the seed, construction alternates between mutation of one parent and crossover of two distinct parents. Binary tournaments based on mean partial validation score select parents from the eligible population; after step 10, the five lowest-scoring variants lose parent eligibility. The resulting graph branches from earlier repositories and combines branches through crossover, allowing prior variants to contribute beyond the next construction step. Validation performance does not improve monotonically. At step 24, crossover combines repositories from steps 2 and 6 to obtain the highest mean partial score, 50.2%50.2\%, compared with 35.8%35.8\% for the seed. Its binary success rate is 26.7%26.7\%, tying steps 5, 25, and 29, compared with 6.7%6.7\% for the seed. Thus, earlier branches remain useful well beyond their construction step, and the two validation metrics distinguish different aspects of repository performance.

Figure 8 shows the corresponding 30-step ScienceBoard run with a 60-minute episode limit. Parent selection uses validation success averaged over the initial evaluation and any repeated evaluations, with denoising every five construction steps as described in Section 7.3. The highest mean belongs to if-016, a crossover of if-014 and if-009: it achieves 71.7%71.7\% success over four evaluations of the 15 validation tasks, compared with the seed’s initial 53.3%53.3\%. Its parents have mean scores of 66.7%66.7\% and 60.0%60.0\%, respectively. Later variants continue to draw on earlier branches, but none exceeds if-016’s mean within the 30 steps. The lineage illustrates how crossover can combine branches with different validation histories while repeated evaluation informs which repositories remain promising.

B.2 Execution Efficiency

Table 6 compares the seed and evolved repository across 108 OSWorld V2 tasks. On each repository’s full-credit tasks, the evolved agent uses 7.1%7.1\% fewer tool calls on average while receiving full credit on more tasks. Together with the CDP case in Appendix B.4, this suggests a useful role for helper functions: reusable operations can reduce repeated setup and combine multiple low-level interactions within a single tool call. Such savings can free steps for task-specific reasoning and execution.

The aggregate comparison also shows why helper-level improvements need not shorten every trajectory. Across all tasks, mean call counts remain nearly unchanged. The full-credit subsets differ, and on the 11 tasks where both repositories receive full credit, the mean rises from 87.8 to 103.2 calls. Excluding the interrupted evolved attempt likewise leaves similar all-task means (163.2 for the seed and 163.4 for the evolved repository). Thus, the shorter full-credit average describes each repository’s successful trajectories rather than a uniform speedup on matched tasks. The CDP trace supplies concrete evidence of reduced setup and bulk-reading overhead; the aggregate results show that these local savings coexist with other sources of task-level variation.

B.3 Examples of Evolved Interfaces

Figure 9 shows how the task agent uses an evolved repository during a task and what its interfaces contain. Table 7 lists interfaces from the evolved repositories described in Section 7, with what each lets the agent observe and do.

B.4 Additional Case Study

We examine how a reusable Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) interface changes browser interaction in a client photo-delivery task. The agent must read instructions in TeamChat, reconcile invoices with payments in VaultBank, and prepare and email either finished photos or watermarked previews. We compare the seed repository with evolved variant if-011 on the same task. The seed provides browser target discovery but lacks a page-evaluation helper, whereas the evolved repository exposes browser.page_eval and browser.page_text for executing JavaScript and retrieving page text through CDP.

Figure 10 shows the requested conversation and the helper operations used to retrieve its text.

Reusing browser access.

The seed agent implements its own CDP client during the task, encountering missing dependencies, an incorrect target identifier, and connection and message-handling failures before obtaining the requested direct message. The evolved interface encapsulates target selection and WebSocket communication, allowing the agent to navigate and read the message using existing helpers. The same message is retrieved by tool cell 11 with the evolved repository, compared with cell 37 for the seed. This illustrates how repository evolution can move browser setup and debugging out of the task trajectory and into reusable code.

Figure 11 contrasts the selected milestones leading to the same message in the two trajectories.

Reading structured page content.

The evolved agent also uses JavaScript to load additional bank transactions and extract 81 table rows from the page DOM. It then aggregates payments by client name in Python. Returning page text and structured records lets the agent process multiple entries in one operation, reducing the need for repeated visual inspection and transcription. The resulting interface supports both navigation and bulk reading through the same browser session.

Table 8 shows a shorter trajectory with fewer tool calls and image-bearing results, alongside a higher task score. The clearest mechanism is reduced browser setup overhead and direct access to page content. Both agents eventually use CDP, so the benefit illustrated here is making that capability readily reusable. The full task also includes file, image, and email operations, and the repositories differ in other interfaces; the overall duration difference is therefore an observed case outcome rather than an isolated estimate of CDP’s effect.

B.5 Tasks With and Without Evolved Interfaces

OSWorld V2 evolution comparison.

Figures 12–16 compare the seed repository with an evolved repository on the same task. The top row of each figure follows the seed episode through the agent’s own screenshots, in order. Red dots mark clicks at the coordinates in the agent’s code, drawn on a screenshot from the calls named under each panel. A stack of frames marks repeated attempts. In the Word case, where the seed agent works almost entirely in code, the later panels quote its code and output. The bottom row shows the evolved episode: the interface documentation the agent read, the call it made, and the output it received. The call and output are quoted from the trajectory, shortened where marked with an ellipsis. The documentation is condensed: function names and signatures are exact, the descriptions paraphrase the docstrings the agent printed, and the functions the agent used are highlighted.

The episodes were selected to illustrate these mechanisms and are not controlled comparisons. Several evolved repositories come from separate evolution runs with the same tasks and model. Call counts exclude the cost of building the interface, and the synthetic s_* tasks are ungraded. Figure 17 additionally compares the bare agent with if-024 on OSWorld V2 task 038.

ScienceBoard evolution comparison.

Figures 18–20 compare the seed repository with the selected evolved repository, if-016, on the same ScienceBoard tasks using the same task model and evaluation harness. The top row (“Without the interface”) follows GUI interactions in the seed episode; the bottom row (“With the interface”) shows the evolved helper documentation, calls, and returned observations. Both episodes pass in each case. Model steps count completed assistant responses, including retries, failed attempts, verification, and the final answer; one step may contain multiple actions. Each condition has one episode per task. These qualitative cases illustrate interface use rather than estimating a treatment effect or isolating an individual helper’s benefit.

Appendix C Harness Prompts

We reproduce the main builder prompts used for repository evolution. Prompt provides the standing instructions for mutation from ungraded synthetic-task trajectories, and Prompt starts each mutation step. Prompt describes how to combine two parent repositories, and Prompt specifies the builder’s execution protocol. These prompts are fixed by the harness rather than evolved with the repository.

# Shadow Interface Builder
You improve software that helps AI agents complete computer tasks on Ubuntu 22.04.
## Evaluation evidence: synthetic tasks without verifiers
These 30 synthetic training tasks (s_001 through s_030) have NO verifiers.
Their dummy evaluators always return 0.0. Zero does NOT mean failure, and
scores/averages do NOT measure task success. Never optimize those numbers,
use them as rewards, or classify all attempts as failures. Raw result.txt
and diagnostic score fields are compatibility placeholders only.
Read the TRAIN trajectories under eval_results/ recursively. Each task folder
contains instruction.txt, claude_trajectory.jsonl (a historical filename also
used for Qwen/Prime traces), and any available diagnostics/screenshots.
The aggregate latest_summary.json and validation trajectories are intentionally
not supplied to the builder. Do not try to access validation data.
Use instructions, actions, tool outputs, screenshots, errors and observed
artifacts to identify repeated work, missing capabilities and fragile workflows.
An agent’s claim that it completed a task is not verified success. Distinguish
observed evidence from hypotheses, and record both in notebook.jsonl. Do not
invent a verifier or labels. Improve the evolving software from trajectories.
## What you can modify
- ‘shadow_interface/‘ — all your code goes here
- ‘shadow_interface/context_compaction.json‘ — evolvable mini-SWE context-window, reserve, keep-recent, and checkpoint-summary policy
- ‘notebook.jsonl‘ — append observations (persists across mutations)
## Constraints
- Python stdlib only — pip is disabled on VMs
- VMs are fresh — no state persists between tasks
- Task agents are autonomous — they may or may not use your tools
- Do NOT modify files outside shadow_interface/ and notebook.jsonl
- Do NOT create or modify SYSTEM_PROMPT.md — the task agent’s system prompt is controlled by the orchestrator
- You do NOT run evals — the orchestrator evaluates after you finish
## Goal
Build general, reusable tools that help agents complete tasks more reliably and efficiently, using trajectory evidence. The orchestrator separately measures each version on the older validation set; synthetic scores remain ungraded.
Two qualities to keep in mind as you build:
- **Generality.** Prefer helpers that work across many tasks. A helper that only addresses one specific task is a sign you stopped one level too early — keep abstracting until the same helper would serve the next, related task.
- **Discoverability.** Write clear signatures and docstrings. Agents find your tools via ‘python -m shadow_interface capabilities‘ and ‘python -m shadow_interface doc <name>‘; helpers without docstrings get passed over for less specialized ones the agent can read.

The mutation turn instruction refers the builder to the standing instructions in CLAUDE.md reproduced above.

Appendix D OSWorld V2 Synthetic Training Tasks

We use 30 synthetic tasks to provide construction experience for Agent S4. The set contains 21 tasks that use desktop applications and nine that involve local mock websites, sometimes together with desktop applications. Each task includes an instruction, input materials, and an initial application state. The tasks cover document and spreadsheet work, media editing, 3D modeling, research, file management, and web workflows. Table 9 lists all task IDs, goals, and applications. Section D.1 gives their full task-specific instructions.

Construction and use.

We used gpt-6-astra for task authoring and gpt-5.6-sol for independent task review. Author agents created original scenarios and materials from environment and coverage briefs. Independent reviewer agents assessed originality against the benchmark and the accepted synthetic bank, coherence, feasibility, and the challenge supported by the materials. This review assessed task design. It did not label agent attempts or create reference solutions. The training package uses a constant-zero evaluator for compatibility with the runner; this placeholder is not a success label or a training reward. The meta-agent receives the resulting training trajectories, while held-out validation determines selection as described in Section 3.3.

Use the attached bench records to prepare an editable LabPlot project and a single-page engineering figure. The three product names in the inventory must be the series labels. Our immediate decision is the 3.00 L/min duty point; use valid measurements whose corrected flow falls within 2.95–3.05 L/min, with no interpolation. A cartridge clears this screening only if its pressure-drop mean PLUS its combined standard uncertainty is at most 24.0 kPa AND its heat-transfer mean MINUS its standard uncertainty is at least 135 W. If no valid point remains in that duty window for a cartridge, label it unassessed. This is a conservative one-standard-uncertainty screening convention for this fictional prototype, not a statistical confidence or safety certification.

Use points with connecting segments only between valid measurements from the same cartridge, in increasing corrected-flow order rather than acquisition order; do not fit a model or interpolate the screening result. Mark the 24.0 kPa and 135 W thresholds and make the duty window understandable without obscuring the data. Axis labels must name quantities and units. Choose ranges that include the entire valid sweep and its uncertainty bars. D.1.24 s_024 Explain Mere Studio’s spring-cart damping comparison

Applications. Shotcut.

Use Shotcut to complete the Mere Studio teaching video described below. Inputs are in /home/user/CUESTraining/cues_r024/inputs/ and this brief is also in /home/user/CUESTraining/cues_r024/production_brief.txt. The timeline has not been started.

MERE STUDIO — Spring-cart demonstration

We need a short silent teaching video for a public mechanics display. Two original schematic recordings show the same spring cart released from the same displacement with different damping. These are illustrative animations, not laboratory measurements. Use only the two supplied MP4s. Cobalt is Damping A; amber is Damping B. The physical cart width and the 100 MM bar are the same in both recordings; their framing is different.

Make an 18–24 second, 1280×\times720, 30 fps comparison in Shotcut:

•A short opening introduces ‘‘Same release, different damping’’ and identifies the footage as an illustrative simulation. • The central comparison places Damping A in the upper panel and Damping B in the lower panel, playing simultaneously at their original speed. Trim away unnecessary waiting, retain about half a second held before release, synchronize the visible release to within two output frames, and show at least ten seconds after release in both panels. The gray lamp turns green when the release jaw withdraws. Confirm alignment from motion as well as the lamp; do not synchronize the raw file starts. • Match physical scale using the visible 100 MM bars: they should appear equally long to within roughly 5%. Align the two vertical REST datums to the same screen x position to within about 8 pixels. Preserve proportions. Keep the moving carts, spring anchor, rest band and scale bars visible throughout. Crop unused source margins and arrange clean, distinct panels, with no footage spilling into the other panel. Panel labels must remain legible and not cover the moving cart or scale bars. Original corner run labels may be cropped away. • Follow the main comparison with a synchronized half-speed replay of a 2–3 second interval that clearly shows the difference around the first passage through rest and subsequent reversal. Choose the interval by inspecting the footage. Enlarge/reframe this replay around the carts and rest bands; keep the two panels at equal physical scale and their rest datums aligned. The spring anchors and scale bars may fall outside this closer crop, but the cart travel during the chosen interval must remain visible. Label the replay ‘‘Half speed’’. • End by holding an informative comparison image for approximately two seconds with one short, plain-language observation supported by what viewers just saw. Mention both overshoot and settling behavior, without inventing measured settling times or presenting a real engineering certification. Keep this readable at normal display size.

Simple cuts are suitable. No sound or music is needed. Do not stretch a clip independently to force correspondence: use synchronized trims for the main view and the same 0.5×\times speed for both replay clips. No external assets are needed. Keep all video, panel placements, text and replay segments editable in the native project.

Save deliverables in /home/user/CUESTraining/cues_r024/output/: damping_comparison.mlt — editable Shotcut project, using the supplied local input paths damping_comparison.mp4 — H.264/yuv420p, 1280×\times720 at 30 fps, silent handoff.txt — brief source in-points used for the synchronized main comparison, source interval used for each replay, and the visual checks you performed. A few lines suffice.

Review the exported picture, especially the release alignment, readable labels, equal cart scale, and whether moving parts stay inside their panels. Leave the native project open in Shotcut.
