Import or convert the SVG into editable Draw shapes as needed and check that individual objects can be selected before proceeding. Follow the brief’s composition, diagram and handoff requirements. Create /home/user/CUESTraining/cues_r029/output/ and save rain-display.odg, the one-page rain-display.pdf and handoff.txt there. Inspect both the native page and PDF before finishing.

D.1.30 s_030 Prepare Mereford’s individualized home-practice letters

Applications. LibreOffice Writer, LibreOffice Calc.

Prepare Measure Together’s home-practice letters using the files in /home/user/CUESTraining/cues_r030. Read production_request.txt, teaching_bank.txt, diagnostic_responses.txt and learner_roster.csv. The home_practice_master.docx is an unfinished editable starting letter, with plain-text placeholders.

Interpret each learner’s responses using the supplied prerequisite and completeness rules. Build a local Calc data source that retains all learners and records the chosen issue/hold state, a concise internal evidence reason, and the individualized teaching content needed for the letters. Follow the consent and incomplete-observation rules. For each issued letter use one appropriate activity from the bank and supportive feedback grounded in that learner’s responses, with no score or public internal labels.

Convert the starting letter into one reusable native Writer merge master with genuine database-backed fields. Suppress optional address lines and the kit paragraph using native conditional/address features. Bind to the saved local data, retain any connector needed to reopen the merge, and produce a single combined editable ODT and PDF in LearnerID order. Follow every requirement in production_request.txt, including one A4 page per recipient, at least 11 pt body text, at least 35 mm clear response space, the correct practice and session details, and consistent recipient data. Inspect the full run and regenerate from the master if anything needs correction.

Save final files together in /home/user/CUESTraining/cues_r030/output/: home_practice_master.odt, learners.ods, home_practice_letters.odt, home_practice_letters.pdf, any required local database connector, and handoff.txt. The handoff should identify held IDs and reasons and explain the local connection and repeat-run procedure. Do not email, send, or physically print anything.

Appendix E ScienceBoard Synthetic Training Tasks

We use 48 synthetic tasks to provide construction experience for Agent S4 on ScienceBoard. They cover the benchmark’s six scientific applications, with 10 for Celestia, 7 for ChimeraX, 9 for GRASS GIS, 10 for KAlgebra, 7 for Lean and 5 for TeXstudio. Each task includes an instruction, an initial application state and, where needed, input materials. The tasks were authored and reviewed as described in Section 4. Of the 50 authored tasks, we exclude sb_chimerax_006 and sb_grassgis_010 because their initialization fails before the task agent starts. The tasks have no evaluators, so attempts are recorded without success labels. Table 10 lists the tasks, and Section E.1 gives the full instructions as the task agent received them.

E.1 Task Instructions

The runner appends the same execution reminder as for the OSWorld V2 synthetic tasks (Section D.1).

E.1.1 sb_celestia_001 One Moon, two viewpoints

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to prepare a two-panel illustration of how the Moon’s apparent phase depends on the observer’s position. Pause time and show the Moon in two side-by-side views at that same instant. In the left panel, make it clearly crescent: less than half of the disk illuminated. In the right panel, make it clearly gibbous: more than half illuminated, but not full. Change the viewpoints rather than advancing time. Keep the entire lunar disk inside each panel at approximately the same apparent diameter. Leave the comparison open and explain in one sentence why the illuminated fractions differ.

E.1.2 sb_celestia_002 A fixed coastline under changing daylight

Applications. Celestia.

In Celestia, set up a running day/night view of Earth in which the Australian mainland stays in the middle of the disk as simulation time advances. Show the whole Earth disk, turn clouds off, and keep the day/night shading clearly visible. Leave time running forward at 1000×\times. The coastline must stay in the same position on screen without further camera adjustments while its illumination changes.

E.1.3 sb_celestia_003 Return to a ring-shadow observing point

Applications. Celestia.

Create a reusable observing point in Celestia for studying Saturn’s shadow on its rings. Set simulation time to 2021-01-01 00:00:00 UTC and pause it. Compose an oblique view with the whole planet and the outer edges of the rings inside the window, making the dark shadow cast by Saturn onto the rings clearly visible. Save this observer state as a native bookmark named ’Ring-shadow observing point’, with the saved simulation time. To check that it can reproduce the observation, go to Neptune and change simulation time to 2031-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, then use the bookmark to return. Leave the restored Saturn view visible and paused at the saved 2021 time, with the same framing and shadow geometry.

E.1.4 sb_celestia_004 Enlarge Mars by magnification and by travel

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to compare two ways of making Mars appear larger. Pause time and prepare one centered, mostly sunlit view of Mars with a field of view (FoV) of 45 degrees. Adjust the observer distance so the whole disk is about one quarter of the graphics viewport’s height; this is your baseline. First, keep the observer at that position and change only FoV until the disk is about half the viewport height. Next, restore FoV to 45 degrees and change only the distance to Mars to obtain a half-height disk again. After establishing the baseline, keep simulation time, viewing direction, and window dimensions fixed, with Mars centered throughout. Report the displayed FoV and Mars distance, including units, for the baseline and each of the two enlarged views. Use these readings to explain briefly how the two enlargement procedures differ. Leave the final 45-degree view open with the whole disk and the FoV and distance readouts visible.

E.1.5 sb_celestia_005 Compare the surface speeds of two slow-turning planets

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia’s built-in object information to compare the rotational surface speeds at the equators of Mercury and Venus. Treat each planet as a sphere with Celestia’s displayed radius, and use its displayed sidereal rotation period. Compare speed magnitudes, ignoring the direction of rotation and any motion of clouds. Report the radius and rotation-period readings for both planets with their units, then calculate the dimensionless ratio v_Venus / v_Mercury to two significant figures. Show the relation you used and identify which planet has the faster equatorial surface despite the difference in their sizes. Base the comparison on Celestia’s displayed values. Leave the faster planet selected and in view, with its radius and rotation period visible in the object information.

E.1.6 sb_celestia_006 Date the light received from Neptune

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to work out when light arriving near Earth just after midnight left Neptune. Set simulation time to 2025-01-01 00:10:00 UTC and pause it. Go to Earth and use that arrival viewpoint as the observing position. Select Neptune without travelling to it, and read Celestia’s light-travel delay from the observer to Neptune. Treat that displayed delay as constant for this exercise. Report the displayed delay with its units and the corresponding light-emission date and time in UTC, rounded to the nearest minute. Briefly explain the relation between the reception and emission times. Set the simulation clock to the emission time you reported and leave Celestia paused with Neptune selected and the UTC date/time readout visible.

E.1.7 sb_celestia_007 View the Summer Triangle from another star

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to investigate whether the Summer Triangle keeps its apparent shape when the observer moves between stars. Its three members are Vega, Deneb, and Altair. Pause time and use Go To Sol to establish the first observing position. Record the displayed distances from there to all three triangle stars, including units. Prepare two equal-sized views at this same paused instant: one at the Sol arrival position and one at the arrival position after Go To Capella. Show all three triangle stars with readable names in both views, using the same field of view. Keep Vega centered in both panels, and orient the Deneb-to-Vega direction the same way on screen in both views. Framing changes must rotate the camera without moving either observing position. Keep constellation diagrams and boundaries off. Compare the triangle’s shape, allowing for an overall rotation or uniform enlargement: does its relative spacing stay the same? Support your answer with a specific comparison of one named star pair’s separation relative to another pair’s separation, then use the three distance readings to explain your observation. A qualitative spacing comparison is sufficient. Leave the two views visible and time paused.

E.1.8 sb_celestia_008 Distinguish orbital direction from rotating-frame motion

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to investigate whether a moon’s apparent motion around Mars can be mistaken for a retrograde orbit. Start at 2025-03-01 00:00:00 UTC with time paused. Prepare two equal side-by-side views looking down on Mars’s north pole, with Mars centered and the complete orbits of Phobos and Deimos in view. Use matching initial observer distances and fields of view. Show both moon names, both orbit paths, and Mars’s planetographic grid. In the left panel, make the observer travel with Mars while its camera axes remain fixed relative to distant stars. In the right panel, make the observer rotate with Mars so its longitude grid stays fixed on screen. Do not track either moon. Run the shared simulation time forward at 10000×\times and watch at least 24 simulated hours without adjusting either camera. For each moon, report its clockwise or counterclockwise motion in each panel, and decide whether its actual orbit is prograde or retrograde relative to Mars’s spin. Explain the observations briefly in terms of the moons’ angular motion relative to the rotating planet. Add a visible object marker only to each moon whose apparent clockwise/counterclockwise sense changes between the two panels. Leave both views visible and running forward at 10000×\times, with the moon names, orbit paths, and grid still shown.

E.1.9 sb_celestia_009 Estimate the selection bias of a magnitude-limited stellar census

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to compare two idealized stellar populations whose members have the same absolute magnitude as Altair or Deneb, respectively. A hypothetical all-sky survey detects a star when its apparent magnitude is at most 6.0. Assume the two populations have equal, uniform number densities; ignore extinction and Galactic boundaries, and treat the catalog magnitudes as fixed. Pause time and use Go To Sol to establish the observing position. Keep that position throughout the task. In the Star Browser, obtain Altair’s and Deneb’s distance, apparent magnitude, and absolute magnitude; report all six readings with distance units. Identify which prototype appears brighter from this position. Using the absolute magnitudes, calculate each population’s maximum detection distance in parsecs and the expected detected-number ratio N_Deneb-like / N_Altair-like. Give distances and the ratio to two significant figures, using unrounded intermediate calculations, and state the relations you used. Briefly explain why the ordering by apparent brightness here need not match the ordering by expected survey detections. Leave the Star Browser visible in Brightest mode, sorted by absolute magnitude from brighter to fainter, with the prototype representing the more numerous detected population selected. Keep time paused and the observer at the Sol arrival position.

E.1.10 sb_celestia_010 Find the latitude where Capella stops setting

Applications. Celestia.

Use Celestia to determine how far north an observer must be for Capella to become circumpolar: never below the ideal horizon during a daily circuit. Compare two observing sites on Earth’s surface, both at longitude 0 degrees, at latitudes 30 degrees N and 60 degrees N. At each site, inspect Capella throughout the simulated interval from 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC to 2025-01-02 00:00:00 UTC, keeping the observer fixed to that surface location. You may turn the camera in place. Show the horizontal coordinate grid and turn off atmospheres and clouds. Use the grid’s altitude-zero circle as the ideal horizon; ignore refraction and terrain. For each site, report whether Capella crosses below that horizon or stays above it throughout the circuit. At 60 degrees N, estimate its lowest altitude to the nearest 5 degrees. Use that estimate to infer, also to the nearest 5 degrees, the northern latitude where Capella’s daily circle would just graze the ideal horizon, and briefly explain the geometric relation used. Leave Celestia paused near Capella’s lowest altitude during the specified interval at the 60-degree-N site, with Capella selected and named, the northern horizon and horizontal grid readable, and the observer still fixed to Earth.

E.1.11 sb_chimerax_001 Separate hinge motion from scaffold displacement

Applications. ChimeraX.

The two open models, support_reference.pdb and support_moving.pdb, are synthetic C-alpha point scaffolds for a geometry exercise, not real proteins. In both, chain A residues 1-7 form a fixed support; chain B residues 1-5 form a lever whose tip is the CA atom of B:5. Superpose the moving model onto the reference using all seven corresponding chain-A CA atoms only. Apply one rigid transformation to the whole moving model, preserving its internal geometry. Then measure the distance between the two B:5 CA tips in this shared support frame. Report that displacement to the nearest 0.01 Å and briefly explain why the lever atoms were excluded from the fit. Leave both full scaffolds visible in distinct colors, with the two tip atoms shown as spheres and a readable distance monitor between them. Save the comparison as /home/user/ScienceBoardSynthetic/sb_chimerax_001/hinge_comparison.cxs.

E.1.12 sb_chimerax_002 Compare two alternate oxygen positions

Applications. ChimeraX.

The open alternate_site.pdb contains invented serine and water geometry for an alternate-location exercise, not an experimental structure. For serine A:7, compare alternate locations A and B of OG with the fixed water oxygen W:1@O. In ChimeraX, report each location’s occupancy and its OG-to-water-oxygen distance to the nearest 0.01 Å, then state whether the higher-occupancy location is also the closer one. Leave the closer OG location active in the original model with a readable distance monitor to the water oxygen. Preserve both stored alternate locations and the original coordinates.

E.1.13 sb_chimerax_003 Screen high-residual sites on a shared scale

Applications. ChimeraX.

The open array_a.pdb and array_b.pdb are invented point arrays for a data-screening exercise, not molecules or experimental structures. Each carbon marker represents one numbered site. Its PDB B-factor stores a synthetic residual magnitude in arbitrary units, and its occupancy stores a sampling-coverage fraction. In ChimeraX, prepare a comparison with all sites shown as spheres and colored by residual using the same continuous scale in both arrays: blue at 0, white at 6, and red at 12, with linear color interpolation between these values. Add a readable matching color key. Select exactly the sites across both arrays whose residual is at least 8 and whose coverage is at least 0.80; high residual alone does not qualify a poorly sampled site. Leave both complete arrays visible with this selection highlighted, preserving their coordinates and stored values.

E.1.14 sb_chimerax_004 Map contacts across two toy edges

Applications. ChimeraX.

The open edge_markers.pdb contains two invented rows of carbon markers, chains A and B, for a geometry exercise; these are not molecules or experimental observations. Each numbered residue is one site. In ChimeraX, find every cross-chain contact using a center-to-center distance of at most 3.50 Å as the sole criterion. Exclude pairs within the same chain and do not use van der Waals overlap as the cutoff. Show all markers as spheres, distinguish the chains by color, and display only the qualifying cross-chain contacts as dashed pseudobonds with readable distance labels. Select all participating sites and leave both complete rows visible without changing coordinates. Report the number of contact pairs and the number of distinct participating sites in each chain; a site with several partners counts only once in its chain’s site total.

E.1.15 sb_chimerax_005 Find the closest sampled approach of two moving markers

Applications. ChimeraX.

In ChimeraX, open /home/user/ScienceBoardSynthetic/sb_chimerax_005/gate_sweep.pdb as one trajectory with nine coordinate sets. This is invented point geometry, not a molecule, experimental structure, or physical dynamics simulation. The C atoms of chain A residue 1 and chain B residue 1 are the two moving tips; the other four markers are fixed reference points. Inspect the tip-to-tip separation across all nine sampled frames. Report the frame with the smallest sampled separation, its labelled time, and its separation to the nearest 0.01 Å. Also report every sampled frame with separation strictly below 4.50 Å. Frame 1 is labelled 0 ps and successive saved frames are 2 ps apart; do not infer an unsampled minimum or a continuous threshold-crossing time. Export all six markers from only the minimum-separation frame to /home/user/ScienceBoardSynthetic/sb_chimerax_005/closest_snapshot.pdb. Leave the full trajectory loaded and paused at that frame, with all six markers visible, the frame slider visible, and a readable distance monitor between the two tips. Preserve all input coordinates.

E.1.16 sb_chimerax_007 Measure the tilt and probe clearance of two fitted panels

Applications. ChimeraX.

The open panel_markers.pdb contains invented point geometry, not molecules or experimental observations. Chains A and B each contain nine carbon markers sampling a slightly nonplanar panel; P:1@C is a separate probe. In ChimeraX, create one native fitted plane for each panel using all nine of that chain’s markers with equal weight. Use orthogonal least-squares fitting, minimizing squared perpendicular distances, and exclude the probe from both fits. Report the smaller angle between the two fitted planes in degrees to one decimal place. Measure the unsigned perpendicular distance from P:1@C to each fitted plane, report both to the nearest 0.01 Å, and identify the nearer plane. Treat the planes as infinite for these measurements; the displayed disk rims are not panel boundaries. Leave both fitted plane disks and all 19 markers visible in a useful oblique view, with each panel and its plane sharing a distinct color and the probe visually distinct. Keep the Axes/Planes/Centroids tool open and preserve the input coordinates.

E.1.17 sb_chimerax_008 Rotate one linker bond while keeping its anchor fixed

Applications. ChimeraX.

The open torsion_linker.pdb is an invented seven-carbon heavy-atom linkage for a geometry exercise, not an experimental or energy-minimized molecule. Its single residue A:1 contains the bonded chain C1-C2-C3-C4-C5-C6-C7. In ChimeraX, measure the starting C1-to-C7 distance, then set the ordered C2-C3-C4-C5 dihedral to +75.0 degrees by rotating about C3-C4. Keep C1, C2, and C3 at their original coordinates; rotate the entire C4-C7 side together about that bond axis, preserving all bond lengths, bond angles, and other internal torsions. Keep exactly the seven supplied atoms and the six supplied bonds. Report the starting and final C1-to-C7 distances to the nearest 0.01 Å and state whether this rotation lengthened or shortened the end-to-end separation. Save the edited linkage in its original model coordinate frame as /home/user/ScienceBoardSynthetic/sb_chimerax_008/linker_75.pdb. Leave the edited linkage fully visible in ball-and-stick style with readable atom-name labels and a C1-to-C7 distance monitor. Keep Build Structure’s Adjust Torsions section open with C3-C4 active, C2 shown as Fixed, C5 shown as Moving, and the final signed angle displayed.

E.1.18 sb_grassgis_001 Meadow access with a wet-ground exclusion

Applications. GRASS GIS.

In this fictional meadow study, equipment can reach ground within 35 metres of the service_track centreline, but must stay inside meadow and outside wet_ground. Using the three existing vector maps, create accessible_meadow containing all qualifying ground, including any disconnected pieces. Use planar distances in the project CRS, with rounded buffer corners and end caps. Save the result in the current work mapset and display it with the meadow outline and service track. Report the total qualifying area in hectares, rounded to two decimal places. The project uses EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with coordinates in metres; all geometry is invented toy data.

E.1.19 sb_grassgis_002 Local height contrast without bridging survey gaps

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing pad_height raster is an invented survey of a small test pad. Create a floating-point raster named neighbor_relief in the current work mapset: for each cell, subtract the arithmetic mean of its eight immediately surrounding cells (four edge neighbors and four diagonal neighbors) from that cell’s height. Exclude the center cell from the mean. Evaluate a cell only when its height and all eight neighboring heights are known; otherwise write NULL, including at the outer boundary. A valid zero contrast must remain zero. Keep the input’s full extent, alignment, and 2 m cell size. Heights are in metres above an arbitrary local datum, and the resulting signed contrast is in metres; positive contrast means locally raised ground. The horizontal CRS is EPSG:32631, with coordinates in metres. Save neighbor_relief as a native raster and leave it displayed in GRASS GIS.

E.1.20 sb_grassgis_003 Map the light sensors needing a repeat visit

Applications. GRASS GIS.

Import /home/user/ScienceBoardSynthetic/sb_grassgis_003/station_counts.csv into GRASS GIS as 2D station points, then create a native point vector named revisit_stations containing exactly the stations with qc = valid, a strictly positive baseline count, and a repeat count at least 20% lower than the baseline count. Include the 20% boundary. Both pulse counts cover equal 60-second intervals; zero is a recorded value. The CSV lists northing before easting: use easting_m for x and northing_m for y. Coordinates are metres in the current EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N) project, and all data are invented. Preserve the selected stations’ original coordinates, station identifiers, counts, and quality flags in the output. Save revisit_stations in the current work mapset and leave it displayed with all its points in view.

E.1.21 sb_grassgis_004 Coarsen a sprinkler map without changing what its values mean

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing wetting_depth and surface_code rasters describe an invented sprinkler plot on matching 2 m grids. Create native rasters wetting_depth_6m and surface_code_6m on a common 6 m square-cell grid covering exactly the original footprint: west 500001, east 500025, south 5100007, north 5100025. Do not expand or shift the footprint. Each wetting_depth value is water depth in millimetres averaged over its source cell, not a per-cell volume. The coarser depth must represent the mean depth over each target cell and preserve the total represented water volume across the plot, without rounding depths to integers. Each surface_code value is a nominal class: 2 = sand, 5 = turf, 9 = paving. For each target cell, retain the code of the surface occupying the greatest area within it; do not blend the codes. There are no missing cells or tied dominant classes. Save both results in the current work mapset and leave surface_code_6m displayed with the entire plot in view. The project uses EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with horizontal coordinates in metres; use planar cell areas.

E.1.22 sb_grassgis_005 Recover slope and downhill direction from a centimetre DEM

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing training_height_cm raster is an invented earthwork surface, with elevations in centimetres above an arbitrary local datum. The horizontal CRS is EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with coordinates and 2 m cell sizes in metres. Create two native floating-point rasters in the current work mapset using GRASS GIS’s Horn 3-by-3 terrain-derivative method: slope_percent, containing slope as percent rise, and downhill_azimuth, containing the direction of steepest descent in degrees clockwise from north. Account for the different vertical and horizontal units. Azimuths must lie in [0,360), with north = 0, east = 90, south = 180, and west = 270; use -9999 for exactly flat cells, whose slope must be zero. Preserve the input’s full extent, alignment, and 2 m resolution. Leave the outermost cell ring NULL in both outputs, without estimating edge derivatives. Save both rasters and leave slope_percent displayed with the entire plot in view.

E.1.23 sb_grassgis_006 Map a cart’s twenty-second service reach

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing cell_time and depot rasters describe an invented cart yard on matching 2 m square-cell grids. Create a native raster named reachable_20s marking every cell whose centre can be reached from the centre of the sole non-NULL depot cell with a minimum accumulated travel time of at most 20 seconds. Set qualifying cells to 1 and all other cells to NULL, including barriers and disconnected ground. The depot starts at elapsed time zero and must be included. Each cell_time value is the time in seconds to traverse one whole cell orthogonally, not seconds per metre. Use the standard eight-neighbor movement model: an edge-neighbor move costs the arithmetic mean of its two endpoint values, and a diagonal move costs that mean times sqrt(2). A move is allowed whenever both endpoint cells are non-NULL, including diagonals past barrier corners; do not use knight’s moves. NULL cell_time cells are impassable, and travel must remain within the input footprint. Minimize travel time rather than geometric distance, and apply the inclusive 20-second limit without rounding accumulated times. Preserve the input extent, alignment, and resolution. Save reachable_20s in the current work mapset and leave it displayed with the entire yard in view. The project uses EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with horizontal coordinates in metres; all data are fictional.

E.1.24 sb_grassgis_007 Retain connected habitat patches large enough for a refuge trial

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing land_cover raster represents an invented refuge trial plot on a 2 m square-cell grid. Codes 3 (grass) and 7 (shrubs) both count as habitat; code 0 is bare ground, code 8 is paving, and NULL means unsurveyed. Create a native integer raster named refuge_patches containing only habitat patches with a planar area of at least 48 square metres, including exactly 48. Treat grass and shrubs as one habitat class when deciding connectivity: cells belong to the same patch if linked through habitat cells sharing an edge. Corner contact alone does not connect patches. Give every retained patch its own positive integer ID, with the same ID throughout that patch; the actual ID numbers are your choice. All other cells must be NULL. Count only habitat cells toward patch area, preserve holes and gaps, and remove small patches without expanding or merging them. Keep the input’s full extent, alignment, and 2 m resolution. Save refuge_patches in the current work mapset and leave it displayed with the entire plot in view. The project uses EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with coordinates in metres. All data and the refuge criterion are fictional teaching material.

E.1.25 sb_grassgis_008 Account for cut and fill only where both surveys exist

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing before_height and after_height rasters describe an invented earthwork trial. Both give cell-average ground height in metres above the same arbitrary local datum on matching 2 m square-cell grids. Create a native floating-point raster named change_m containing after minus before, retaining a value only where both heights are known. Keep valid zero change as zero and all other cells NULL; preserve the input extent, alignment, and resolution. Then create a native area vector named block_budget with the same three polygons and category IDs as work_blocks. For each block, add numeric attributes surveyed_m2 (the area with both heights known), cut_m3 (positive volume removed where ground became lower), fill_m3 (positive volume added where ground became higher), and net_m3 (signed fill minus cut). Integrate height change over planar cell area, treating each cell average as constant across its cell. The block edges follow grid edges, so include whole cells only. Use the same jointly surveyed cells for all four attributes, including unchanged cells in surveyed_m2; do not fill survey gaps or extrapolate to unsurveyed parts of a block. Ignore soil bulking and compaction, and keep full calculation precision in the stored attributes. Save both results in the current work mapset and leave change_m displayed with block outlines and the block_budget attribute table open. The horizontal CRS is EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with coordinates in metres. All data are fictional teaching material.

E.1.26 sb_grassgis_009 Map redundant sightlines across a teaching plot

Applications. GRASS GIS.

The existing terrain_m raster and observation_posts vector describe a fictional visibility trial. Create a native integer raster named sightline_coverage classifying every terrain cell: 0 = visible from neither post, 1 = from A only, 2 = from B only, and 3 = from both. Use each post’s eye_m attribute as its eye height above local ground, and test a target 0.75 m above local ground at every terrain cell centre. Use GRASS GIS’s native r.viewshed terrain model, looking in all directions with no distance limit; ignore Earth curvature and atmospheric refraction. Terrain is the only obstruction. Keep the DEM’s complete extent, alignment, and 4 m resolution; all terrain heights are known, so keep class 0 as zero rather than NULL. Report the percentage of the full plot’s planar area visible from both posts, to one decimal place. Save sightline_coverage in the current work mapset and leave it displayed with the observation posts overlaid and the coverage classes distinguishable. The horizontal CRS is EPSG:32631 (WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N), with coordinates in metres; terrain heights are metres above an arbitrary local datum. All inputs are invented teaching data.

E.1.27 sb_kalgebra_001 Minimize coating cost for an open channel

Applications. KAlgebra.

An idealized open-top channel has a rectangular internal cross-section with area 3.6 cm2. Its width w and wall height h are both positive. For each unit length of channel, coating the bottom costs three times as much per unit area as coating either side wall. Ignore wall thickness and end walls. Use KAlgebra to express the coating cost as a function of width alone, normalized by the side-wall coating price per unit area and by channel length. Find the width and wall height that minimize this cost, and report both to the nearest 0.01 cm with a brief explanation of why your choice is a minimum. Keep the numerical dimension calculations in the calculator history. Leave the 2D Graph tab visible with the cost curve and its positive-width minimum clearly in view.

E.1.28 sb_kalgebra_002 Overlay a delayed actuator pulse

Applications. KAlgebra.

Use KAlgebra to plot two command profiles for a toy actuator model. The horizontal coordinate x is time in seconds and the vertical coordinate is command level in arbitrary units. The first profile is zero through x = 1, rises linearly to level 4 at x = 3, stays at level 4 through x = 5, falls linearly to zero at x = 8, and stays zero thereafter. The second profile has exactly the same shape, delayed by 1.5 seconds and with every command level multiplied by 0.7. Represent each complete profile as one piecewise function, including its zero portions. Leave the 2D Graph tab visible with both profiles enabled in different colors and the viewport set to x from -1 to 11 and y from -0.5 to 4.5.

E.1.29 sb_kalgebra_003 Orient a corrugated-sheet surface

Applications. KAlgebra.

Use KAlgebra to model an idealized corrugated sheet as a height surface z = f(x,y), with x, y and z measured in centimetres. The corrugation is sinusoidal about z = 0, with amplitude 0.6 cm. Its straight, parallel crest lines run in the direction (3,4) in the xy plane, and the perpendicular distance between neighboring crest lines is 4 cm. The sheet passes through the origin, and its height initially increases when moving from the origin along positive x. Construct and plot the height function in 3D. Leave the 3D Graph tab visible in Lines style at an oblique angle that clearly shows the parallel crests and troughs and their height variation. State the height function you used.

E.1.30 sb_kalgebra_004 Recover inputs from an ambiguous calibration

Applications. KAlgebra.

A toy instrument uses the calibration r = ((x-1)*(x-5))^(1/2), where x is restricted to the interval [0,6] and the exponent denotes the nonnegative real square root. Use KAlgebra to find every admissible input x that produces the reading r = 2. Keep numerical substitution checks for every returned input, using unrounded values, in the Calculator history. Leave the 2D Graph tab visible with the calibration curve plotted in a viewport of x from 0 to 6 and y from 0 to 3, so the real-domain branches can be inspected. Both x and r are dimensionless.

E.1.31 sb_kalgebra_005 Separate travel along a guide from transverse drift

Applications. KAlgebra.

An invented motion-tracking sample has instantaneous velocity v = (4, -1, 3) mm/s in fixed orthogonal x, y, z axes. Its intended travel line has direction d = (2, 3, 1); d is dimensionless and is not a unit vector. Use KAlgebra to decompose v into a velocity vector parallel to this line and a perpendicular drift velocity vector whose sum is v. Report both vectors in x, y, z order and the magnitude of the drift velocity, all to three decimal places in mm/s. Keep the calculations in the Calculator history, including checks with unrounded values that the two vectors reconstruct v and that the drift vector has zero scalar product with d. E.1.32 sb_kalgebra_006 Find the first successful dilution cycle

Applications. KAlgebra.

In an invented mixing experiment, a well-mixed vessel initially holds 12 L of water containing 18 mg of a conserved tracer. Each cycle drains 3 L, refills with tracer-free water to 12 L, and then adds 1.2 mg of tracer in negligible volume, mixing fully before the next cycle. No other tracer loss occurs. Use KAlgebra to find the smallest whole number of completed cycles after which the tracer concentration is strictly below 0.55 mg/L. Cycle 0 means the initial vessel; evaluate concentration only after complete cycles, including the added dose. State the recurrence or equivalent expression you used, and report the cycle number and the concentrations after that cycle and the immediately preceding cycle. Give concentrations to three decimal places, but use unrounded values to decide the strict inequality. Keep the calculations and both threshold comparisons in the Calculator history, and leave the Calculator tab visible.

E.1.33 sb_kalgebra_007 Account for recording bias in bead energy

Applications. KAlgebra.

An invented bead stream has four possible speeds: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 m/s. Their incoming population proportions are given by the relative weights 7, 9, 5, and 3, respectively. Every bead has mass 4.0 g. A detector records an incoming bead with probability 0.10, 0.35, 0.80, or 0.95, respectively, conditional on its speed; recording does not change the bead’s speed. Treat all supplied values as exact for this toy model. Use KAlgebra to calculate the expected translational kinetic energy of a randomly selected recorded bead. Use K = m*v^2/2 with consistent units. Report the expected energy in millijoules to three significant figures and briefly explain how you weighted the four speed classes after recording. Keep the weighting and energy calculations in the Calculator history, and leave the Calculator tab visible.

Overlay the directrix as a second graph in a different color. E.1.35 sb_kalgebra_009 Fit a colorimeter calibration with a free baseline

Applications. KAlgebra.

Use KAlgebra to calibrate an invented colorimeter from five teaching measurements. The standard concentrations c are 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 mmol/L; their corresponding dimensionless absorbances A are 0.035, 0.210, 0.401, 0.562, and 0.758. Treat the standard concentrations as exact. Fit the affine model A = a + b*c by ordinary least squares, minimizing the sum of squared absorbance residuals with equal weight for all five standards. Fit the intercept a as well as the slope b. Then use this fitted model to estimate the concentration of an unknown sample whose absorbance is 0.487. Report the fitted intercept and slope to four decimal places, with units where applicable, and the unknown concentration to three significant figures in mmol/L. Use unrounded fitted coefficients for the concentration calculation. Keep the fitting and concentration calculations in the Calculator history, and leave the Calculator tab visible.

E.1.36 sb_kalgebra_010 Compare interior and transition errors in harmonic reconstruction

Applications. KAlgebra.

Use KAlgebra to investigate a toy square-wave reconstruction. The ideal voltage has period T = 2.4 s: it is +1.5 V for 0 << t << T/2 and -1.5 V for T/2 << t << T, repeated periodically. An N-term reconstruction adds the first N odd sine harmonics. For k = 1,…,N, harmonic k has frequency (2*k-1)/T Hz, amplitude 4*1.5/(pi*(2*k-1)) V, and zero phase. Construct the reconstructions for N = 4 and N = 12. For each reconstruction, calculate the signed percentage error relative to +1.5 V at two locations: the fixed interior time t = T/4, and the near-transition time t = T/(4*N), using that reconstruction’s own N. Define this error as 100*(reconstructed voltage - 1.5)/1.5. Report all four signed errors to one decimal place, identifying the reconstruction and sampling location, and briefly compare how the interior and near-transition errors change when more harmonics are included. Use unrounded intermediate values and keep the reconstruction evaluations and error calculations in the Calculator history. Leave the 2D Graph tab visible with both reconstructions and the +1.5 V reference line enabled in three distinct colors. Use the horizontal coordinate x for time in seconds and set the viewport to x from 0 to 1.2 and y from -0.2 to 2.0 V.
